title: I Said to My Scattered Self, Gathering It In
intro: The diwan dates these verses to 395 AH (1004–05 CE), when al-Sharif al-Radi set out for Wasit to meet his father returning from Fars. His thoughts on the road turn to people whose friendship and protection proved illusory. Doors refuse to open, water dissolves into mirage and a trusted shield reveals where its bearer can be hurt. He vows to leave these people behind, but his verses will still make the journey back to them.

translation: I said to my scattered self, gathering it in,
“How long this knocking at every sealed door?”
1.sharh: The speaker has to gather his own scattered purposes before he can address himself. Knocking at one closed door after another gives that dispersal a physical history.

translation: It is time to disobey my desires and willingly obey
despair, which gathers my scattered affairs.
2.sharh: Despair of these people can be a means of recovery. The man who obeys it regains the integrity that his many hopes have cost him.

translation: The covetous man dies without fulfilling a single need,
forever keeping himself going on empty pretexts.
3.sharh: One Arabic verb serves for dying and for accomplishing a purpose. Death completes its business while the covetous man completes none of his.

translation: Tell the people I tested and found
a mirage: something other than a mirage slakes my thirst.
4.sharh: The mirage is discovered by travelling to it. His test of these people has cost a similar expenditure of hope and effort.

translation: I prepared you to fend off every calamity
from me, and you aided every calamity.
5.sharh: The calamity stays in exactly the same verbal position at the end of each half. What changes sides is the help he had counted on.

translation: I took you for my shield. It was as though
the enemy saw my vulnerable places through my shield.
6.sharh: A shield ought to hide the body’s vulnerable places. People entrusted with his safety knew enough about him to show an enemy precisely where to strike.

translation: Reports that let the envious cool his burning thirst,
and, whenever unearthed before an enemy, make him gloat.
7.sharh: News of the humiliation travels beyond the original gathering. Thirst is at last quenched, but it belongs to the envious listener who relishes the story.

translation: Fruit refuses to be fine
when the branches of its great tree are mean in origin.
8.sharh: He had expected generous fruit from these people. Looking back towards the roots, he finds a reason for the failure in the very nature of the tree.

translation: When I cast my hopes towards you,
conflicting impulses multiplied and tossed my judgement about.
9.sharh: The hopes fly straight towards their objects. His judgement, by contrast, is pulled first one way and then another.

translation: I stood before you like a man pulled apart,
fearing death, hoping for his wish.
10.sharh: Death and desire sound almost alike in Arabic. In that small space between the two words he has to decide whether to advance.

translation: One foot makes towards you and the other turns
away. Sound judgement belongs to the deliberate.
11.sharh: The feet act out his divided intention. At the close he finds there may be some wisdom in refusing to take the next step too quickly.

translation: Without reversals I would have gained no experience.
Green wood hardens, and the young horse gets its mature teeth.
12.sharh: Experience changes his substance, as green wood hardens with age. The second verb names a stage that a horse reaches when a later tooth comes through.

translation: Despair turned the course of my requests away from you
and twisted my mount’s neck towards home.
13.sharh: Giving up hope supplies a direction. One turn of the mount’s neck puts the whole journey on the road home.

translation: I have no excuse except to leave you.
Once I go, give up hope of my return.
14.sharh: Departure is the only account he means to give. The hopelessness he once felt about them will become theirs when they look for him again.

translation: I will leave as one who never grieves
to part from you, never glancing back.
15.sharh: The backward glance is the bodily gesture of lingering attachment. He vows that neither his feeling nor his movements will betray it this time.

translation: I will shake my hands free of hope in you
as fingers shake free of earth from a dead man’s grave.
16.sharh: The hands have finished with this hope as finally as hands that have just buried someone. Dust on the fingertips brings the gesture startlingly close.

translation: I will flash every far-travelling verse
as an Indian blade flashes in a swordsman’s right hand,
17.sharh: The poet can leave while his verses go on travelling. The glint of a drawn sword gives the threat of an unforgettable line a visible edge.

translation: each rhyme trotting towards you
with its flame, at the trot of a horse let loose.
18.sharh: The rhyme carries fire and moves like a riderless horse. The man’s own mount has turned away, but his poetry runs straight at its target.

translation: I tell the heart still tugging towards you,
“Curb your desire. You have had trouble great and small.”
19.sharh: The oath of departure has not quite silenced the heart. A proverbial pair of feminine forms, one a diminutive, collects trials of every size into one warning.

translation: Can I shake what will not bend or turn someone
who will not desist, or blame someone deaf to shame?
20.sharh: The three efforts move inwards, from bending a body to turning a will and finally touching a conscience. Blame does no good when the capacity for shame is absent.

translation: What a waste of the hope I directed
in greed towards those people. What a waste of me.
21.sharh: One brief correction in the middle of the second half changes the object of lament. What he squandered was himself.

translation: And those ships travelling by night, at whose bows there curls
a wave like the humps of full-grown camels.
22.sharh: The night passage evokes the journeys spent in pursuit of these men. Camel humps give the rolling sea a contour familiar to someone accustomed to travelling overland.

translation: People who, when they attend the assembly in disgrace,
sneeze without anyone wishing them well.
23.sharh: Courtesy ordinarily answers a sneeze with a blessing. Withholding even that tiny acknowledgement makes the men’s social standing unmistakable.

translation: Time, enough. You have struck my vital places.
You have always sought my unguarded moment through fate.
24.sharh: Time becomes the adversary who has at last found an opening. The vulnerable places recall what the faithless shield exposed near the beginning.

translation: Why lay on anyone else what
decree upon decree has done, when you are my affliction?
25.sharh: He has used his sharpest words on particular people. The closing address to Time asks whether even his blame has been directed at the wrong door.

1.1.4.head: الشَّعاع
1.1.4.meaning: Scattered in purpose, pulled apart by conflicting concerns.

1.2.3.head: القِراع
1.2.3.meaning: Knocking repeatedly at a door for admission.

1.2.6.head: مُصمَت
1.2.6.meaning: Sealed or solid, offering no opening.

2.2.3.head: شَمل
2.2.3.meaning: The things one holds together, here the unity of one’s purposes.

3.1.5.head: أُربَة
3.1.5.meaning: A need one wants to satisfy.

3.2.4.head: تَعِلَّة
3.2.4.meaning: Something that keeps a person going while waiting, a diversion or consolation.

4.2.1.head: آل
4.2.1.meaning: A mirage that looks like water to the thirsty.

4.2.4-5.head: نَقَعَ الغُلَّة
4.2.4-5.meaning: “Quenches my burning thirst”: satisfies a long-felt need.

5.1.4.head: مُلِمَّة
5.1.4.meaning: A calamity that descends upon someone.

6.1.3.head: جُنَّة
6.1.3.meaning: A shield or protection. Its vowel distinguishes it from the word for a garden.

6.2.3.head: مَقتَل
6.2.3.meaning: Vital spots where a wound can be fatal.

7.1.1.head: سُمَع
7.1.1.meaning: Reports that go about and make a person known, sometimes to their cost.

7.2.2.head: نَبَثَ
7.2.2.meaning: Were dug up or brought out, of reports aired before an enemy.

9.2.2.head: الخِلاج
9.2.2.meaning: The play of conflicting thoughts tugging at a person.

10.2.2.head: المَنِيَّة
10.2.2.meaning: Death, set beside the similar-sounding word for a wish.

11.1.2.head: أَمَّ
11.1.2.meaning: Makes straight for you, takes you as its destination.

12.2.1.head: عَسا
12.2.1.meaning: Hardens after being green and pliant, said of wood.

12.2.3.head: قَرَحَ
12.2.3.meaning: A young horse reaches an age recognised by its teeth. Both editions give this verb. The reciter appears to say yatrah, “casts off”.

12.2.4.head: الجَذَع
12.2.4.meaning: A young animal, here a horse not yet mature in its teeth.

13.1.3.head: سَنَن
13.1.3.meaning: The course or bearing of a road.

13.2.5.head: مَطِيَّة
13.2.5.meaning: A riding mount, especially a camel used on a journey.

16.2.2.head: أَنمُلَة
16.2.2.meaning: Fingertips, where the dust of burial has clung.

17.1.3-4.head: بَيتٌ شارِد
17.1.3-4.meaning: “A wandering verse”: one that gets abroad and circulates by word of mouth.

17.2.5.head: المُصلِت
17.2.5.meaning: Someone who has drawn a sword from its sheath.

18.1.4.head: خَبَّ
18.1.4.meaning: Trots briskly, the gait of a horse.

18.2.1.head: شُواظ
18.2.1.meaning: A tongue of flame carried here by a verse of invective.

19.2.4-5.meaning: “The little one and the one”: an idiom for troubles great and small.

20.2.2.head: اِرعَوى
20.2.2.meaning: Draws back or desists on taking heed.

20.2.6.head: اِختَتى
20.2.6.meaning: Shrinks back in shame, the gloss recorded by Ibn Aydamir.

22.1.1.head: سُرى
22.1.1.meaning: The ships’ night passage, one of the journeys he has wasted. Both printings have this reading. The recording can also sound like “and you see the ships”.

22.2.4.head: الجِلَّة
22.2.4.meaning: Full-grown or aged camels with prominent humps.

23.1.4.head: النَّدِيّ
23.1.4.meaning: The place where the community gathers to talk or consult.

23.2.2.head: مارِن
23.2.2.meaning: The soft part of the nose, here standing for the nose that sneezes.

23.2.4.head: مُشَمِّت
23.2.4.meaning: One who blesses a person after a sneeze. The same root earlier meant gloating over an enemy.

24.2.4.head: المَقادِر
24.2.4.meaning: The strokes of fate allotted to someone.

24.2.5.head: غِرَّة
24.2.5.meaning: An unguarded moment, when vigilance has slipped.
